title: Is Hanuman alive?
hookLine: two torches crossing a battlefield at night, and an old bear's surprising question
carry: sankat mochan: in trouble, hindus call on hanuman
last: MARYADA: LINES RAMA WON'T CROSS, EVEN TO WIN.

cards: Two people are still on their feet: Vibhishana, who knows the weapons of Lanka, and Hanuman. It's night.
They take torches and walk out across the battlefield, stepping between fallen warriors, looking for anyone still alive. Rama and Lakshmana lie in the arrows. Leader after leader lies still.
Then, in the torchlight, they find Jambavan, the old king of the bears, so pierced with arrows he can't open his eyes, still breathing.

teach.b: Vibhishana kneels and asks if he's alive. Jambavan knows the voice, though he can't see. And his first question isn't about Rama, or Lakshmana, or Sugriva his king.
It's this: is Hanuman alive? Vibhishana is puzzled. Why Hanuman, and not the princes?
Jambavan's answer is short and startling.

teach.h: IF HE LIVES, WE ALL LIVE.
teach.b: If Hanuman lives, the whole army lives, even if it has been killed. If Hanuman is dead, we're dead, though we're still breathing. Hanuman steps forward and bows at the old bear's feet.
Jambavan gives his orders. Go north, over the ocean, to the Himalaya.

teach.h: FOUR HERBS ON A HIMALAYAN PEAK.
teach.b: Between Mount Rishabha and Mount Kailasa is a mountain covered with healing herbs. He names four: one that brings back life, one that draws out arrows, one that restores the body's color, one that joins what's broken.
Bring them, and the army will rise. Why ask about Hanuman first? Because Jambavan knows who can still save them.
That same trust lives in one of Hanuman's best-loved names: Sankat Mochan, the remover of troubles.

When trouble comes, at a hospital door, before a surgery, on a frightening night, many Hindus say Hanuman's name first, and the Hanuman Chalisa sings that he frees from trouble whoever holds him in mind, word and deed.
Many also believe Hanuman is a chiranjivi, one who lives on, still near wherever Rama's name is sung. So the old bear's question has an answer devotees give gladly: yes.

how: Devotees call Hanuman Sankat Mochan, the remover of troubles, and turn to him in emergencies; Jambavan's question, is Hanuman alive, is often retold as a sign of his place in the Ramayana.

s: he asks whether Hanuman is alive, and explains why.

games.q: you're Jambavan, wounded and blind on the battlefield at night. you hear a friend's voice. what's your first question?
games.why: he asks about Hanuman: if Hanuman lives, the army lives even though slain. it's the same trust devotees put in Hanuman as Sankat Mochan.

practice: Bring to mind someone you know who's in trouble right now. If you pray, say Hanuman's name slowly with the breath, or the familiar Jai Hanuman, holding that person before him.
If you don't, ask Jambavan's question for them instead: who, and what, can still help? Let the breath steady you while you wait for the answer.

wordCard.voice: Lakshmana wounded. While the princes lie in the arrows, Jambavan asks first whether Hanuman lives: the seed of his name Sankat Mochan, the remover of troubles.

orig.note: Sanskrit Jāmbavān: the old king of the bears, an elder of the army, also called Jāmbavat.

carryVoice: Your line: sankat mochan, in trouble, Hindus call on Hanuman. A flight north before dawn comes next. That's day six hundred forty-eight.
